title: Iran reportedly fortifies nuclear sites as it prepares for possible U.S. strikes after midterms
description: Residents continue their daily routines across business centers, shopping districts, and city streets despite escalating tensions between Iran and the
body: Residents continue their daily routines across business centers, shopping districts, and city streets despite escalating tensions between Iran and the United States on October 12, 2026 in Tehran, Iran.Fatemeh Bahrami | Anadolu | Getty ImagesIran is reportedly working to bolster its military capabilities in preparation for possible renewed U.S. attacks after the November midterm elections.The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that the Islamic Republic has been strengthening defenses around sensitive locations like nuclear sites, and telling regional officials that Tehran will respond to any new U.S. strikes with retaliatory measures across the Middle East. The Journal's report also said the Iranian regime is preparing its population for war by holding rallies, sending paramilitaries to read war stories to young children and advertising training in firing defensive missiles. U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that American forces would not attack Iran before the midterm election, which will take place on Nov. 3.The Iranian and U.S. governments did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the Journal report.Houthi attacks on RiyadhMeanwhile, a Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis – a Yemeni militant group backed by Tehran – said it had intercepted a ballistic missile shot at Riyadh, the Saudi capital, on ⁠Monday, news agency Reuters reported.The Houthis have been attacking the Saudi capital since last week, launching multiple strikes on energy facilities and airports. One airport attack resulted in multiple deaths, including a pilot working for Saudi carrier Saudia. The closure of King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh has been extended until Saturday. On Monday, the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration urged airlines to exercise caution when flying above or near Saudi Arabia.Iran-linked U.K. base threatU.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham told British lawmakers on Monday that an attempted attack on an air force base in England was "almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard."Ed Miliband, the U.K.'s foreign minister, said he had summoned the Iranian ambassador to stress that "Britain will not tolerate threats on our soil."British police arrested five men on Sept. 27 on suspicion of terrorism offenses over an alleged threat to RAF Fairford in the west of England, a Royal Air Force base that the U.S. Air Force has used to strike Iranian missile sites.Trump later said the U.S. had moved all its long-range bombers out of the U.K. in response to "a threat."

schema.headline: Iran reportedly fortifies nuclear sites as it prepares for possible U.S. strikes after midterms

title: Six Flags shares decline following deadly roller coaster incident
description: UKRAINE - 2021/08/25: In this photo illustration the Six Flags Entertainment Corporation (Six Flags Theme Parks) logo is seen on a smartphone screen.
body: UKRAINE - 2021/08/25: In this photo illustration the Six Flags Entertainment Corporation (Six Flags Theme Parks) logo is seen on a smartphone screen. (Photo Illustration by Pavlo Gonchar/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)Sopa Images | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesShares of Six Flags Entertainment declined more than 14% Tuesday following a deadly roller coaster incident at one of its amusement parks in Georgia.One person died and several others were injured Monday in an incident at Six Flags Over Georgia, according to a statement from Georgia's Cobb County Board of Commissioners. The board's chairwoman, Lisa N. Cupid, said that county authorities are working with Six Flags and other partners in the investigation. According to reports citing local police, the incident occurred on the Atlanta-area park's 200-foot-tall Goliath roller coaster shortly before 4 p.m. Monday. Riders were later seen being evacuated from the roller coaster after it stopped near the top of the ride, according to the report. Witnesses told a local news station that they saw a man fall from the roller coaster and strike the ride several times. A park spokesperson for Six Flags Over Georgia told CNBC that the park team is cooperating with local authorities and providing support to those affected by the tragedy, and that Six Flags Entertainment is temporarily closing Georgia's Goliath and nine other similar attractions at its parks. "We were deeply saddened by the guest incident at one of our parks yesterday. Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest's family, friends, and loved ones," the spokesperson said.

schema.headline: Six Flags shares decline following deadly roller coaster incident

title: Williams says Fed may not have to hike rates in 2027, at odds with traders
description: John Williams, president and chief executive officer of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, during a Bloomberg Television interview in New York, US,
body: John Williams, president and chief executive officer of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, during a Bloomberg Television interview in New York, US, on Tuesday, April 7, 2026. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesNew York Federal Reserve President John Williams said Tuesday that he doesn't see additional rate hikes in 2027 after one more increase this year."I haven't changed my view that it may be appropriate to have one more rate hike," Williams said in an interview with Bloomberg News. "I don't think at this time I have any reason to believe that we would need to do more."Williams' comments place him at odds with the market and some other members of the central bank. Fed funds futures traders are largely betting that the central bank will raise rates at least once in 2027, according to CME's FedWatch data as of Tuesday. Latest trading gave about 90% odds that the Fed overnight rate would end 2027 at least a half percentage point higher than where it is today.The New York Fed head is also at odds with many Federal Open Market Committee members, though he is still in-line with the majority. Eight of the 18 who gave a rate forecast for 2027 see one more increase after an additional hike this year. Williams is a permanent voting member of FOMC, the body that decides where interest rates should be set at each Fed policy gathering.The Fed in September issued its first rate increase since 2023. Fed officials indicated plans for another hike in meeting minutes, but did not clarify when. The central bank meets at the end of this month and then one more time in December.To be sure, Williams told Bloomberg that "we'll have to see" when it comes to forecasting into the new year."This economy is being affected by lots of different influences, and we just have to keep watching the data," Williams said.'Disinflationary' trendsWilliams said the Fed should look at "underlying trends" in inflation amid price shocks tied to energy and artificial intelligence.While the former San Francisco Fed chief cautioned that energy prices continue to put upward pressure on overall inflation, he said they could provide relief on an annual basis in the future. Williams also said that effects of tariffs on price growth have mostly been seen.He said overall inflation for 2027 should be "near" the Fed's target of 2% on an annual basis. The personal consumption expenditures price index, the Fed's favored inflation gauge, in August showed a 12-month increase of 3.4% or 3% if stripping out food and energy prices."I still believe there's disinflationary forces at play. Those I don't think have fundamentally changed," Williams said. "In fact, my forecast for inflation for next year is inflation to come down quite a bit."— CNBC's Matt Peterson contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Williams says Fed may not have to hike rates in 2027, at odds with traders

title: Kimberly Guilfoyle resigns as ambassador to Greece at White House's request
description: Newly appointed US Embassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle arrives at the Greek Presidential Palace to present her credentials to the Greek President
body: Newly appointed US Embassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle arrives at the Greek Presidential Palace to present her credentials to the Greek President in Athens, on November 4, 2025. Aris Messinis | Afp | Getty ImagesU.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle said Tuesday she would resign, shortly after new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said Guilfoyle was being asked to leave her post."While my time as Ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end," Guilfoyle said in an X post.Guilfoyle also broadly denied "recent allegations" against her, apparently referring to multiple critical articles in The Wall Street Journal about her conduct before and after becoming an ambassador, which had prompted questions about her job security."These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity," Guilfoyle said in the post. "I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service."Asked for comment on Guilfoyle's post, a Wall Street Journal spokesperson told CNBC, "We stand by our reporting."President Donald Trump suggested later Tuesday morning that the reporting on Guilfoyle's conduct prompted the call for her resignation."She was doing a good job, but we didn't like what we were reading," Trump told reporters outside the White House before boarding Marine One.The president also pushed back when a reporter noted that Guilfoyle, who was previously engaged to Trump's eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., was almost a member of his family."No, she wasn't a member of my family," Trump replied. "She, I guess, dated my son a long time ago, but she wasn't."Hours earlier, Zacharia revealed that the White House had urged Guilfoyle to step down."We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign," Zacharia said while taking questions from reporters in the White House briefing room for the first time. "She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well."Trump had signaled Monday evening that Guilfoyle could be on the chopping block."Well, we're looking at it," Trump said at the White House when a reporter asked if he was weighing firing the ambassador."Yeah, we're not happy," he added.Guilfoyle's yearlong tenure in Athens was rocked last month by the first of multiple Journal articles on conduct that has raised alarms among ethics experts and former government officials. A Sept. 25 article alleged Guilfoyle persistently promoted a Greek company and involved a lobbyist for a Greek construction firm in meetings with foreign officials.Her attorney, Jesse Binnall, told the Journal in response to that article that Guilfoyle has "worked with companies across the energy sector" and has not been focused on one company.According to an Oct. 7 report from the Journal, Guilfoyle asked Trump donor Eric Deters in July 2025 to wire $100,000 to quietly pay down her American Express bill before her congressional hearing to become an ambassador.Binnall told the newspaper that Guilfoyle had been paid to speak at events prior to being nominated and "was owed a balance for traveling to and supporting these patriotic events." Binnall also disputed the authenticity of messages from Guilfoyle reported in the article, but declined to provide specifics, according to the Journal.On Saturday, the Journal reported that Guilfoyle in January boasted of her close ties to wealthy Greek businessmen as she sought an invite to a dinner being held for Eric Trump, another of the president's sons.

schema.headline: Kimberly Guilfoyle resigns as ambassador to Greece at White House's request

title: The latest inflation data is expected to show price increases are accelerating
description: Customers shop at a grocery store on Sept. 10, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois.Scott Olson | Getty ImagesWednesday's closely watched reading on consumer pri
body: Customers shop at a grocery store on Sept. 10, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois.Scott Olson | Getty ImagesWednesday's closely watched reading on consumer prices could show intensifying inflationary pressures as energy costs keep climbing.Economists polled by Dow Jones expect the headline consumer price index for September to rise 0.6% for the month and to increase 3.6% compared with a year ago. That 12-month number would signal that the rate of price growth is accelerating and moving further from the Federal Reserve's goal of 2%.So-called core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, is expected to increase 0.2% from August and 2.5% on a 12-month basis. While that would mark a slight slowdown from the prior month, it would be an uptick in year-over-year inflation.Upside risk Oil-related prices could drive the headline figure even higher, said Joe Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM, a tax firm. Energy costs have been among the biggest drivers of inflation since the U.S. war with Iran began earlier this year. President Donald Trump last week announced loosened diesel restrictions on Russia in a bid to juice the global oil trade, though analysts don't believe it will meaningfully bring down prices.Prices for Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, climbed more than 14% in September, bringing its third-quarter advance to about 42%. Brent prices on Tuesday traded around $105 per barrel."We've got real upside risk on the September CPI," Brusuelas said. "Typically, when we have these moves in inflation, everyone's models undershoot the actual outcome."Sticky oil prices could also push up costs for items in other, non-energy categories, according to Robert Sockin, chief U.S. economist at asset manager PGIM. In this scenario, it would become harder for the Fed to write off the energy prices surge as a short-term shock that won't necessitate interest rate increases.After announcing its first increase in three years last month, the Federal Reserve signaled in its minutes from that meeting that it will likely have to hike rates again. Fed funds futures traders anticipate the central bank will next lift rates at its December policy meeting, according to CME's FedWatch tool."The list of reasons to hike rates in our view is long," Sockin said. "Ultimately, we have low confidence in the timing of the Fed's next move, but more conviction on the direction of travel."Wednesday's release is the last reading on CPI before November's midterm elections, which could determine whether the Republican party will keep total control in Washington.Economic confidence across political affiliation has fallen this year, according to the University of Michigan's consumer sentiment data. Compared with Democrats, Republican and independent voters have posted steeper declines in sentiment since the start of 2026, the data shows.Economists forecast that the producer price index, a gauge of inflation facing wholesalers due on Thursday, will rise 0.6% from August to September and 5.5% on a 12-month basis. Both of those numbers would mark a modest acceleration in growth compared with August's release.

schema.headline: The latest inflation data is expected to show price increases are accelerating

title: Walmart to cover some GLP-1s, inhalers and insulin for employees at no cost as it expands benefits
description: Walmart logo sign is seen in Chicago, Illinois, Aug. 3, 2026.Marcin Golba | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesWalmart plans to cover more than 250 prescriptions,
body: Walmart logo sign is seen in Chicago, Illinois, Aug. 3, 2026.Marcin Golba | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesWalmart plans to cover more than 250 prescriptions, including some insulin, inhalers and GLP-1s for diabetes, at no cost to its employees in 2027, the company confirmed to CNBC on Tuesday. The retailer is also expanding existing benefits and adding new ones to attract and retain workers at a time when many other employers are offsetting rising healthcare costs with higher prices and scaled-back plan benefits. The announcement comes weeks before open enrollment for Walmart employees closes on Nov. 6.Walmart, the biggest private employer in the U.S., will offer Novo's diabetes injection Ozempic and Eli Lilly's rival shot Mounjaro without charge for people with Type 2 diabetes after a new prior authorization. But the company still does not cover GLP-1s from Novo and Lilly for the purpose of weight loss. Other large employers similarly don't cover those treatments for obesity or have recently dropped coverage to tamp down on their healthcare costs. The latest benefit changes build on Walmart's yearslong effort to boost employee compensation after previously receiving criticism for the healthcare benefits and wages it offers. Walmart employs roughly 2.1 million associates worldwide, with about 1.6 million of those workers based in the U.S., as of the end of fiscal year 2026.In a statement, the company said it's minimizing premium increases for its employees, raising rates for its starting plan by $1.50 per pay period to $39.80. Walmart told CNBC that's a smaller increase than the company made last year. The company is also expanding an existing benefit that pays for employees to see cancer specialists at the Mayo Clinic or the Cleveland Clinic, according to a Tuesday letter to workers from Donna Morris, Walmart's chief people officer. Starting next year, employees under most plans can use that benefit to get a second opinion from a specialist for rare conditions such as ALS, multiple sclerosis and Parkinson's. Among the other added benefits is up to 12 weeks of neonatal intensive care unit leave for parents, which can be added on top of regular parental and maternity leave, the letter said."The steps we're taking are based on years of planning and trying new things, which is allowing us to make meaningful improvements for associates without slashing benefits or significantly raising premiums," Walmart said in its statement to CNBC.

schema.headline: Walmart to cover some GLP-1s, inhalers and insulin for employees at no cost as it expands benefits

title: Bank of America fined $1.2 billion over money-laundering violations
description: A Bank of America branch in New York, US, on Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesBank of America was hit with more than $1.
body: A Bank of America branch in New York, US, on Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesBank of America was hit with more than $1.2 billion in federal penalties Tuesday after regulators said the nation's second-largest bank failed for years to report more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions and fix longstanding anti-money-laundering problems.More than $1 billion of the unreported activity involved national security and other high-priority risks, including Chinese money-laundering networks and activity tied to the southwest border, Treasury said in a press release.The action also lands less than a day before the bank reports quarterly earnings Wednesday morning.Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, which enforces anti-money-laundering rules, said the $1.2 billion penalty is the third-largest in Treasury history. Treasury separately announced an $11.6 million settlement over sanctions violations.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconBank of America Corp. stock priceAs part of the settlement, Bank of America admitted that it willfully violated the Bank Secrecy Act by failing to maintain a compliant anti-money-laundering program, conduct required due diligence on foreign correspondent accounts and file suspicious activity reports, according to Treasury."Today's actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in the press release.Bank of America said in a statement to CNBC that the bank has invested billions in compliance and is "far along" in remediation efforts.The bank said the penalties will result in a $1.2 billion non-tax-deductible charge in its third-quarter results, reducing net income by about 17 cents per share. It said remediation costs are already reflected in its current expense base."Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right," spokesperson Christa Robinson said.The bank's stock was down about 2% in after-hours trading on the news.The new penalties will put renewed focus on the record of longtime CEO Brian Moynihan, who took over in 2010 and spent the early years of his tenure resolving tens of billions of dollars in mortgage-related legal and regulatory matters tied largely to decisions made before he became CEO.For much of the past decade, Moynihan has emphasized what he calls "responsible growth," as Bank of America sought to distance itself from the risk-taking and legal problems that followed the 2008 financial crisis.Moynihan is scheduled to appear on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" at 10:20 a.m. ET Wednesday following the bank's earnings report.Treasury says BofA "prioritized its revenues"Treasury said the bank "prioritized its revenues" while minimizing the impact on compliance resources. The agency said the bank relied so heavily on law-enforcement inquiries and referrals from other financial institutions that regulators said it effectively outsourced part of its responsibility for detecting suspicious activity. The penalty from Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network came in coordination with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, or OCC, an independent bureau within the department, which announced a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America.That sum, which is credited as part of the $1.21 billion total, is the largest penalty OCC has ever levied, the office said.The office accused the bank of serious violations of the Bank Secrecy Act and anti-money laundering rules, and of failing to fix its deficiencies in accordance with a cease-and-desist order it signed in 2024. "Despite its obligation to the American people as a national-chartered, global systemically important bank, the bank's BSA/AML compliance program continues to reflect widespread breakdowns in internal controls, which threatens U.S. national and economic security," Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould said in the OCC press release."The bank's poor response to its BSA deficiencies is unacceptable. The second largest bank's egregious and continued BSA violations warrant the OCC imposing its largest [civil money penalty] ever assessed against a bank," Gould said. "The OCC expects all banks to have an effective BSA/AML compliance program. Those that do not can expect swift and significant action from the OCC."The 2024 order had identified a "breakdown" in Bank of America's systems for detecting and reporting suspicious activity, including a "systemic failure" to set appropriate thresholds for triggering investigations. It also said the bank had failed to make "acceptable substantial progress" correcting an earlier customer due diligence problem.Treasury said the failures included red flags involving possible narcotics-trafficking proceeds, fraud and potential trade-based money laundering that were not addressed in a timely way. Bank of America will also be required to conduct a third-party review for suspicious transactions that went undetected and undergo independent reviews of its transaction-monitoring and customer due-diligence programs, Treasury said.– CNBC's Hugh Son contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Bank of America fined $1.2 billion over money-laundering violations

title: JPMorgan Chase blocks outside AI agents like Muse, Instinct from directly accessing accounts
description: Jamie Dimon, CEO of JP Morgan, and Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta.Getty ImagesJPMorgan Chase won't allow outside artificial intelligence agents to acces
body: Jamie Dimon, CEO of JP Morgan, and Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta.Getty ImagesJPMorgan Chase won't allow outside artificial intelligence agents to access customer accounts and operate on their behalf, CEO Jamie Dimon said Tuesday, citing risks to the company and its customers as tech firms including Meta release autonomous assistants. "We're not going to allow just any … outside agent to come in inside the company, because it's just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan," Dimon told analysts on the bank's third-quarter earnings call."You don't want rogue agents, and it could be thousands of them," he added, describing the potential threat to customers. In July, an OpenAI model hacked into AI company Hugging Face's servers.  The stance from Dimon, the longtime CEO of the biggest U.S. bank by assets and a de facto spokesman for the U.S. financial sector, is reminiscent of an earlier fight with fintech firms over access to customer data. JPMorgan moved to charge data middlemen including Plaid for access, a dispute that similarly pitted the bank's security concerns against tech firms' demands for access.A JPMorgan spokeswoman confirmed to CNBC that the bank currently blocks external AI agents from operating on behalf of retail customers."Protecting our customers is our top priority. Because it is not safe, we do not permit third parties to access accounts by obtaining customers' banking credentials and logging in on their behalf," the spokeswoman said."We support secure, customer-authorized data sharing through open banking providers and are committed to enabling agentic connections securely," she added.That means that AI agents can access some customer data from Chase accounts in a read-only fashion, such as customer balances, if Plaid or another connector has the user's credentials. But they can't send money or pay a bill — actions that make an agent useful.There's no timeline for when the bank would have safeguards in place to allow agents to directly interact with customer accounts, the spokeswoman added.'Liability transfer'Dimon said JPMorgan is using AI agents internally and plans to deploy them for customer-facing applications. The bank's approach, he said, isn't about being for or against the technology, but about ensuring it serves customers safely.In recent weeks, JPMorgan began a targeted pilot for its own AI tool called Smart Cash, which aims to predict a user's cash flow and move funds to maximize yield, Chief Financial Officer Jeremy Barnum said Tuesday. That would appear to be a defensive move against external agents.Dimon also seemed to draw a line about liability when customers authorize outside AI agents to act on their behalf. "If people are using them, they should understand the risk," Dimon said. "They should understand there's a liability transfer."Personal agents have gained mainstream popularity in recent months as AI models integrate more autonomy, like the ability to cancel subscriptions or use credit cards on a user's behalf, for example.Instinct, a digital concierge that relies primarily on text messaging instead of an app, launched earlier this year on an invitation-only basis. The startup behind the service, San Francisco-based Spear Street Technology, was founded last year and reached a $10 billion valuation last month.  In September, bank stocks were hit as Meta's Muse agent topped the app download charts shortly after it was unveiled, sparking fears that consumers would use agents to move funds from low-yielding accounts to higher-yielding ones. Weeks later, OpenAI released its own agent, Dots. Apollo Chief Economist Torsten Slok and others pointed to the risks that agents pose to cheap bank deposits. But that risk will be limited if agents aren't allowed to operate freely with customers' accounts.

schema.headline: JPMorgan Chase blocks outside AI agents like Muse, Instinct from directly accessing accounts

title: Paul Tudor Jones is bullish on oil, says it could rally another $20-$25 because of Iran conflict
description: watch nowHedge fund manager and notable commodity trader Paul Tudor Jones says oil is set to take another leg higher because of the U.S.-Iran conflict
body: watch nowHedge fund manager and notable commodity trader Paul Tudor Jones says oil is set to take another leg higher because of the U.S.-Iran conflict."I am long oil... bullish oil...I think it can rally another $20 or $25 bucks," said Tudor Jones, founder and chief investment officer of Tudor Investment, on CNBC's "Squawk Box." "If something to ameliorate the situation was going to happen, it would have happened already before the midterms."A rally of that size in U.S. oil prices from current levels would send them above their previous closing high for 2026 of just under $113 per barrel. Western Texas Intermediate crude futures were trading at around $92.50 Tuesday morning. Tudor Jones said if the rally were to happen, the equity market would "absolutely totally hate it," though equities were able to relatively manage higher oil prices earlier in the year. The S&P 500 only fell just over 7% at its trough in late March after the start of the U.S.-Iran war on Feb. 28, which was lower than analysts estimated would happen based off of oil's surge. Paul Tudor Jones, founder and chief investment officer of Tudor Investment, speaks with CNBC's Squawk Box on Oct. 13th, 2026. CNBCU.S. oil prices jumped in March after the start of the war, and hit their peak in early April. Prices then fell in June, falling below $70 per barrel that month. However, they started rising again in July, as the conflict in the Middle East heated up again and the status of the Strait of Hormuz — a critical passageway for oil — remained unclear. Prices hit a recent high of almost $106 per barrel in September, though have traded off those levels since. Oil prices are just one headwind that Tudor Jones thinks the equity market needs to handle at the moment. He said 2027 in particular may be difficult for the stock market as investors digest increased equity supply from megacap tech IPOs, like that of Anthropic and OpenAI. While Tudor Jones thinks it's too late before the U.S. midterm elections for a resolution to the conflict, he believes that President Donald Trump will seek to seek peace after voters cast their ballots. "I assume the president has a plan post-election," he said. "I assume he has a plan because, clearly, what's going on is untenable. It's not sustainable, I don't think, in the long-run."

schema.headline: Paul Tudor Jones is bullish on oil, says it could rally another $20-$25 because of Iran conflict

title: Paul Tudor Jones says 2027 could be a really challenging year for the stock market
description: watch nowLegendary hedge fund manager Paul Tudor Jones told CNBC that next year could be a tough one for the stock market because of increased equity
body: watch nowLegendary hedge fund manager Paul Tudor Jones told CNBC that next year could be a tough one for the stock market because of increased equity supply from big tech initial public offerings coming down the pipe as well as a potential reckoning from the ballooning U.S. fiscal deficit. "2027 is going to be really, really challenging for the stock market," Jones told "Squawk Box" on Tuesday. "You've probably got the most negative flow picture for the U.S. stock market that we've had, say, since 2002."The founder and chief investment officer of Tudor Investment said that corporate buybacks, along with mergers and acquisitions, have been a tail wind for the stock market for most of this four-year bull market as they decreased the equity supply. That tide is now turning against the market with major offerings ahead in the AI space from Anthropic and OpenAI, along with one just finished for SpaceX. There will also likely be more secondary offerings from companies in order to raise money for the AI build-out, said Jones. It all adds up to an increased equity supply picture that could weigh on prices.The billionaire hedge fund manager's comments come as investors worry that a bull market now in its fourth year could start to dwindle and run out of steam as concerns grow around mounting inflation, higher bond yields and a more hawkish Federal Reserve. Jones repeated that the current period in the market is akin to 1999, just about a year before the dot-com bubble burst in 2000. He noted the bifurcation in the current market between those companies benefiting from the AI boom and those that aren't. Deficit concernHe also added that a ballooning fiscal deficit is among the dangers for the current stock market, for which he thinks there could be a reckoning.  "We're never going to fix these deficits until the market makes us to. It's going to be just like 2008 and TARP [Troubled Asset Relief Program]. So that's the reality. No politician is going to voluntarily raise taxes or cut spending. They're going to be forced to," he said. "And the only question is, are we now at that tipping point where the market's about to do that? And if you put a gun to my head, I'd say 60-40, we're down that path," Jones said. Oil, which he is long, is another headwind for the market, according to the hedge fund manager. He contended that prices could rally another $20 to $25 after the midterms, a scenario that the stock market will "hate" if it comes to pass. "I'll be short the whole year. There just — there's little value," Jones said. "You had all this issuance, all these IPOs in '98 and '99, and really 2000, 2001, 2002. Those were the easiest years to be short because you kept having these unlocks that just kept adding supply to the market."

schema.headline: Paul Tudor Jones says 2027 could be a really challenging year for the stock market

title: Airport attacks put aviation in crosshairs of geopolitical conflicts
description: Surveillance footage shows people reacting amid smoke at the moment of an attack at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, October
body: Surveillance footage shows people reacting amid smoke at the moment of an attack at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, October 10, 2026, in this frame from a handout video.Saudi Ministry of Media | ReutersDeadly attacks on Saudi Arabia's second-busiest airport over the past week are highlighting how conflicts in the Middle East are upending air travel on a larger scale.Aviation is increasingly in the middle of these sprawling clashes as threats and outright attacks have forced airlines to quickly cancel flights throughout the Middle East for days, weeks and, in some cases, months. Some carriers might redeploy planes that would be going to some Middle East destinations like Dubai, United Arab Emirates, and Doha, Qatar, to other locations altogether."It's a new paradigm. Civil aviation is being directly targeted and it has not been the case in the last couple of decades," said Mark Zee, founder of OpsGroup, an independent aviation safety group whose members include pilots, dispatchers, airline employees and others. The Saudi airport attacks, claimed by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis, were the deadliest in the country in more than a decade. Over the weekend, at least 13 people were killed and more than 300 injured when a projectile hit terminals at King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, officials said. Other attacks have included drones."Historically, airport security is focused on preventing unauthorized access to aircraft and the airport, not defending airspace," said Jeff Price, a professor at the Metropolitan State University of Denver's Department of Aviation and Aerospace Science and an airport management consultant.The threats to aviation are forcing officials to rethink how to protect blind spots in these major public spaces."There is this established way to deal with kind of more conventional weapons such as missiles. It's very expensive, but there is a way," said Gulnaz Ukassova, UAE-based security director of information and analysis at risk management firm International SOS. "There is still no sort of foolproof way to deal with the threat posed by drones. The technology, obviously, is constantly evolving."King Khalid International Airport has been shut down for much of this week, and some carriers suspended operations there, citing safety concerns. CEOs of major oil companies also pulled out of an energy conference in the country. Delta Air Lines, meanwhile, was less than two weeks away from launching an Atlanta-Riyadh route, the first nonstop commercial flight between the the two countries operated by a U.S. airline, according to the carrier.But late Sunday, the Federal Aviation Administration warned U.S. carriers about safety-of-flight risks when flying in or over Saudi Arabia. On Monday morning, Delta said it would postpone the route's debut until March. The new Delta route comes as Saudi leadership seeks to boost tourism to the country, part of the kingdom's Vision 2030 plan to diversify the economy from oil and attract international investment. Air traffic in Saudi Arabia had been increasing rapidly. Scheduled growth in airplane seats in the market is up more than 23% this year from 2023, though the rise has recently slowed, according to aviation-data firm Cirium.Whether travelers come back to the region depends on risk appetite. Ukassova said energy companies, which can depend on in-person visits to large projects, tend to have higher risk tolerance, while academics have a low bar for potential risks.Longer routes, cut flightsThe conflicts have cut off big parts of airspace in the Middle East, mainly over Iran. The outbreak of the Iran war in February set off massive aviation, travel and safety crises.For example, Australian carrier Qantas has changed its Perth, Australia-to-London route to avoid Iranian airspace. Because that flight is then longer, the carrier has added a stop in Singapore to refuel.For four years, Western commercial passenger and cargo planes have already had to fly longer routes to avoid Russian airspace. Carriers started detouring away from Russia after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Taking longer routes to avoid potentially dangerous airspace has been adding to airlines' fuel bills, which got even more expensive this year due to those same Middle East conflicts.While much of the traffic to Dubai and Doha has rebounded from the first days of the war since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, it remains below 2025 levels, according to flight-data firm OAG. Capacity by seats across the Middle East is down 5.7% in October from last year, 2.2 million fewer seats, OAG reported.Some airlines are opting to stay away from the region altogether."We will not fly to Dubai and Doha, and we need to wait until the situation gets settled," Finnair CEO Turkka Kuusisto told reporters last month in New York. title: French supermarket fridges get hacked, heating to 122°F and sparking fires
description: A customer enters an Intermarche supermarket in Issy-les-Moulineaux, on the outskirts of Paris, on October 12, 2026, , following a cyberattack affecti
body: A customer enters an Intermarche supermarket in Issy-les-Moulineaux, on the outskirts of Paris, on October 12, 2026, , following a cyberattack affecting the French supermarket chains Intermarche and Cooperative U that caused their refrigerators to defrost. Dimitar Dilkoff | Afp | Getty ImagesHackers targeted hundreds of French supermarkets in a cyberattack that reportedly caused refrigerators and freezers to overheat, spoiling food and sparking fires. Fridges at French supermarket chains Carrefour, Monoprix, the Les Mousquetaires-owned Intermarché, and Coopérative U, among others, all saw fridges heat up to as much as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) overnight, Reuters reported Monday. Coopérative U's CEO, Dominique Schelcher, confirmed that cyberattacks had affected "refrigeration production facilities of several stores." "Attacking equipment that is essential to the preservation of fresh products and the food supply of the French people is extremely serious and unprecedented. It is unacceptable," Schelcher said in a LinkedIn post. watch nowCNBC has reached out to Carrefour, Monoprix, Intermarché, Coopérative U and E Leclerc for comment but did not immediately hear back.Felix Aime, a senior cyberthreat intelligence analyst ​at Sekoia Threat Detection and Research, said the attack affected several European countries, including Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium, according to the Reuters article. "I strongly condemn the cyberattack targeting food products at @intermarche @CooperativeU @Leclerc," European Commissioner for Agriculture and Food Christophe Hansen said in a post on X on Monday. "Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponization of food has become a reality." AI enhancing cyberattacksLes Mousquetaires said it was expecting the damages, which affected around 180 stores, to reach "several million euros in losses," in an email to CNBC. It said some fresh and frozen food displays have been out of service after the cyberattack affected one of its service providers responsible for managing refrigeration systems inside some stores. TOPSHOT - A woman walks past empty fresh-food refrigerators at an Intermarché supermarket in Névez, western France, on October 12, 2026, following a cyberattack affecting the French supermarket chains Intermarché and Cooperative U that caused their refrigerators to defrost.Fred Tanneau | Afp | Getty Images"Intermarché and Netto have taken all necessary precautions to remove and dispose of any affected products as quickly as possible, to ensure consumer safety," the Les Mousquetaires spokesperson said. "In some stores, the overheating of equipment resulted in smoke, but no fires have been reported."They're now awaiting findings from a court-appointed bailiff and insurance experts to get more precise figures on damages. Stop & Shop parent Ahold Delhaize, which owns popular Dutch supermarket chain Albert Heijn, said that it was experiencing a "security issue within its network," and that systems had been taken offline. It said its stores are still open. This comes amid a broader wave of cyberattacks and cybercrimes, which experts are warning are being enhanced by artificial intelligence. British online fashion retailer Asos experienced a cybersecurity breach last week which revealed some customers' personal information.Meanwhile, a small power plant in the U.K. was shut down for four days in July after a cyberattack which was suspected to be linked to Iran.Interpol's global chief information security officer, Bjorn R. Watne, recently told CNBC that AI can be used to target multiple victims at once, and is increasing the scale and speed of cyberattacks. "It's an evolution and not a revolution."Correction: Bjorn R. Watne is global chief information security officer at Interpol. An earlier version misspelled his name.

title: Judge says Musk engaged in intimidation of ex-FEMA CFO Mary Comans, clears her name
description: Elon Musk, alongside Secretary of Treasury Scott Bessent (L) and Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick (C), speaks during a press event with US Preside
body: Elon Musk, alongside Secretary of Treasury Scott Bessent (L) and Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick (C), speaks during a press event with US President Donald Trump in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC, on May 30, 2025. Allison Robbert | AFP | Getty ImagesA federal magistrate judge in Virginia ruled that Elon Musk engaged in "state sanctioned intimidation" of ex-FEMA CFO Mary Comans when he posted falsehoods on X last year accusing her of "criminal action" and of "funneling $58 million to illegal migrant hotels in Manhattan." Musk, the world's richest person, was working for the Trump administration as the head of DOGE when he shared those posts on Feb. 11, 2025. The Department of Homeland Security said the next day it was firing Comans and three colleagues, and labeled them "deep state activists." In Tuesday's order, U.S. Magistrate Judge William Fitzpatrick cleared Comans' name.Comans served as FEMA CFO from around January 2018 until February 2025, and was also FEMA's operating chief from 2020 to 2021. Fitzpatrick wrote in the order that, "The facts establish that high-ranking government officials," including Musk, then a special government employee, had "engaged in a coordinated public relations campaign to impugn the personal and professional integrity of Ms. Comans.""Mr. Musk was the head of DOGE, he knew or should have known that any payments made to state or local governments through a FEMA grant in February 2025 were approved by his subordinates," the judge wrote. He added that Musk posted a picture of Ms. Comans "to his millions of followers while falsely characterizing her government service as a 'criminal action,'" an act Fitzpatrick described as "little more than state sanctioned intimidation."CNBC has reached out to Musk and White House attorneys involved in the case for comment.Democracy Defenders Fund, which was involved in Comans' case, said in a statement that it was pleased with the decision. "Mary Comans served in the federal government for 21 years," said Craig Becker, the group's head of affirmative litigation. "Career public servants are people, not pawns, and no one who has devoted their life to serving the American public should have their good name destroyed for partisan, political gain."WATCH: Musk says jobs are going to change because of AIwatch now

schema.headline: Judge says Musk engaged in intimidation of ex-FEMA CFO Mary Comans, clears her name

title: Trump census plan to cut noncitizens from 2030 count spurs critics toward legal fight
description: A sign encouraging participation in the U.S. Census lies on a sidewalk in Somerville, Massachusetts, U.S., August 4, 2020.Brian Snyder | ReutersCongre
body: A sign encouraging participation in the U.S. Census lies on a sidewalk in Somerville, Massachusetts, U.S., August 4, 2020.Brian Snyder | ReutersCongressional Democrats and civil rights groups are concerned about a proposed Trump administration change to the U.S. census that would exclude noncitizens without permanent resident status, altering congressional representation and potentially how federal funding is distributed.Opponents warn the rule, which was posted in September, could have negative effects, potentially shifting congressional power to parts of the country where fewer immigrants live and underfunding education, healthcare, food assistance and emergency management programs. The public can comment on the rule until Nov. 2, the day before Election Day."The greatest likelihood is that this is going to end up in litigation," said Meeta Anand, senior director of census and data equity at the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights. "I'm under no delusion that we will see everything remedied because I do know that it's been a project of the administration to exclude noncitizens from the count."The proposed census change is the latest volley in the Trump administration's push to reduce illegal immigration. If certain categories of immigrants living in the U.S. are not counted, areas where they are concentrated could get less federal money. The rule's supporters say counting all immigrants living legally in the U.S. encourages illegal immigration.The rule would exclude from the census millions of noncitizens without a green card, including people in the country on student visas, people with temporary protected status, refugees and asylum seekers. It would also bar the collection of demographic information on race and ethnicity from the census's short-form questionnaire. That information can be used for civil rights enforcement and to assess compliance with federal laws that bar racial discrimination.The White House referred CNBC to the Commerce Department, which oversees the census, when asked for comment on the proposed rule. The Commerce Department and the Census Bureau did not respond to multiple requests for comment.Critics argue the proposal flies in the face of the 14th Amendment, which states, in part, that "representatives shall be apportioned among the several States according to their respective numbers, counting the whole number of persons in each State.""This rule is yet another attack on democracy by Donald Trump," Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said in a statement after the rule was announced last month. "An accurate census count is at the very foundation of ensuring equal representation across our country and delivering federal funds where they're needed most. The Census is enshrined in our Constitution and not up for political debate."Census has counted noncitizens since U.S. foundingProponents, including some congressional Republicans who have introduced legislation to end the counting of noncitizens, argue the census practice of counting all U.S. residents — which dates back to the nation's founding — encourages illegal immigration and makes some voters more powerful than others. "Republicans have long warned that Democrats' intentional illegal invasion and sanctuary policies are rooted in a desire to boost blue states' power," Rep. Andrew Clyde, R-Ga., said in a statement in September announcing legislation that would call for reapportioning congressional seats before the 2028 election while excluding noncitizens and adding a citizenship question the 2030 census. The proposal has 42 Republican co-sponsors.Normally, seats are reapportioned every 10 years using new census data."Amid high stakes and slim margins, Congress must act before the 2028 elections to ensure only American citizens decide how congressional maps are drawn and who resides in the White House," Clyde added.Sen. Bill Hagerty, R-Tenn., introduced similar legislation last year that would require the Census Bureau to include a citizenship status question on any future census, arguing noncitizens heavily skew the congressional map."While people continue to flee Democrat-run cities, desperate Democrats have back-filled the mass exodus with illegal immigrants so that they do not lose their seats in Congress or their electoral votes, hence artificially boosting their political power and in turn diluting the power of other Americans' votes," Hagerty said in a statement.Next U.S. census is in 2030The census changes are not final, but any change the administration implements would be difficult to undo before the 2030 census.The administration in its proposal states that "the Census Bureau is considering how best to distinguish between foreign citizens in the United States who are counted for apportionment" and suggests it would use administrative records to check the legal status of those counted. The proposal also says that the Census Bureau could add an immigration status question to the census' short-form questionnaire.The first, Anand said, would likely have the effect of suppressing response rates and contribute to an inaccurate count. The second would likely lead to errors and the wrongful discounting of people in the country with legal status.A New York Times analysis of the proposal found that it would result in lost House seats in several states, including places that generally favor Republicans. Florida, Rhode Island and Texas would all stand to lose a seat, according to the Times, while Minnesota, Ohio and Oregon could each add a representative to their congressional delegations.But beyond apportioning congressional seats, the rule could reduce funding for federal programs aimed at low-income populations, such as Medicaid, the Children's Health Insurance Program, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and Head Start, said Julie Morita, president and CEO of the Joyce Foundation, a nonpartisan philanthropy that supports racial equity and economic mobility in the Great Lakes region. She noted these programs amount to "trillions of dollars.""An inaccurate count risks a decade of consequences," Rep. Grace Meng, D-N.Y., said in a statement in September. "Census data help determine representation in Congress, electoral districts, and the allocation of federal resources for health care, education, infrastructure, and other essential services." Trump has tried to exclude noncitizens beforeIn the waning days of his first term, Trump attempted to exclude undocumented immigrants from congressional apportionment, though the change wasn't implemented. In August 2025, Trump announced in a TruthSocial post that he'd instructed the Department of Commerce to "begin work on a new and highly accurate CENSUS.""People who are in our Country illegally WILL NOT BE COUNTED IN THE CENSUS," Trump posted.The Commerce Department has authority over the count, but must present to Congress any changes in subjects and the types of information to be compiled at least three years before the next Census Day, which would set an April 1, 2027, deadline. The department is also required to report to Congress the questions that will be included in the census at least two years before Census Day.Congress does have the authority to overrule proposed changes with legislation. But unless Democrats win a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate, overruling the Trump administration is unlikely.A Democratic president who wins election in 2028 could also introduce a new rule to cancel out Trump's exclusion of certain immigrants, but the rule-making process is time-consuming and cumbersome, and there would be little time."Planning for the census takes lots of time, effort, research, operational changes, programming of computers, developing code," Anand said.

schema.headline: Trump census plan to cut noncitizens from 2030 count spurs critics toward legal fight

title: Don't let inflation bite — how to hedge with TIPS, commodities and infrastructure funds
description: J Studios | Digitalvision | Getty ImagesInflation will be in the crosshairs Wednesday as investors digest the latest Consumer Price Index. The reading
body: J Studios | Digitalvision | Getty ImagesInflation will be in the crosshairs Wednesday as investors digest the latest Consumer Price Index. The reading may be one more sign that inflation remains a problem that isn't going away.It's a tricky situation for investors looking for protection, but there are some good ways to get it. Treasury Inflation-Protected securities (TIPS) are one option with "real" yields now at multi-decade highs. Beyond TIPS, analysts suggest commodities, infrastructure, and other assets that can  hedge against rising prices.While inflation is down sharply from its 9.1% peak in 2022 — a  supply shock due to the Covid pandemic — it's still well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target. The headline Consumer Price Index is expected to hit 3.6% in September, partly due to rising energy costs stemming from the war with Iran. The Personal Consumption Expenditures index, the Fed's preferred gauge, was at a 3% core rate in August.Americans' inflation concerns are also rising. The New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations showed the one-year inflation outlook in September climbed to 3.9%, its highest level since May 2023.TIPS deserve a second look Despite their name, TIPS haven't provided much inflation protection this year. The iShares TIPS Bond ETF, which tracks the ICE U.S. Treasury Inflation Linked Bond Index, has a total return of -1.16% year-to-date. Like most other bonds, TIPS have been hit hard by rising interest rates — with the 10-year Treasury note recently hitting multi-year highs around 5.3%. Bond prices and yields move inversely, and as rates climbed many TIPS funds suffered.But rising yields have made TIPS more attractive. The 10-year TIPS yield is currently at 2.87%, after closing at 2.951% on Oct. 5, levels not seen since November 2008, according to Tradeweb.  "Given where rates are, it's getting interesting," says Jason Draho, head of asset allocation Americas at UBS Global Wealth Management. Stock Chart IconStock chart icon10-year TIPS yield year to dateTIPS pay a fixed coupon, or interest rate, but as inflation moves higher, the principal value of the bond increases. The adjustments reflect changes in inflation, based on the non-seasonally adjusted CPI for All Urban Consumers, with a three-month lag. The upshot is that TIPS investors earn interest on a higher principal value over time. That's the essence of the protection compared to traditional Treasuries.TIPS' poor performance this year isn't because of a surge in inflation expectations. Almost all the increase has been due to rising real yields — the nominal yield minus expected inflation.  Real yields are up because of factors like robust economic growth and a U.S. fiscal deficit around 6% of gross domestic product (requiring far more government borrowing).If nominal rates were rising just due to inflation, then TIPS total return — a mix of yield and price — would be fine, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. But that isn't the case."TIPS have produced losses in total return because their income accruals have been insufficient to offset the price decline produced by the rising underlying real yields," Gallo explained. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconiShares TIPS Bond ETF year to dateTIPS maturing in 10 years or more are highly sensitive to duration risk, Draho notes. "You're making a big call on rates not rising any further if you buy TIPS, especially longer maturities of 10-year plus," he said. The bull case is that inflation comes down quicker than expected. That's not the market's expectation, based on short-term Treasury yields, notes Draho. But if inflation does ease next year, which he expects, the yield curve would adjust lower.One way to manage duration risk is to own individual TIPS rather than a fund that has to maintain duration consistent with a benchmark index. Investors could create a TIPS bond ladder with varying maturities, pegged to their income needs over the next decade, for instance. If you hold a TIPS to maturity you may experience price volatility, but you'll get the original principal or inflation-adjusted price, whichever is greater, when the bond matures. Short-term TIPS provide more protection against rate increases and they look attractive, said PIMCO portfolio manager Greg Sharenow."While as a firm, our view is that inflation will ultimately come down, that view keeps on being pushed out as real world events unfold," he said. "We've seen over and over again the last five to seven years — where we're now in our third supply shock — that you end up actually underpricing versus realized inflation," he added.Funds focusing on short-term TIPS include Vanguard Short-Term Inflation-Protected Securities ETF, iShares 0-5 Year TIPS Bond ETF and PIMCO 1-5 Year US TIPS Index ETF.Stocks and other hedgesTIPS, of course, aren't the only way to go. Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, suggests a multi-pronged strategy, including equities, commodities, and alternative assets.  "I'd start layering in more income, keep interest-rate exposure moderate, and then what a lot of people are doing is use things like alternatives to to create more balance in a portfolio," he said. "That makes a lot of sense to me."Broad inflation-protection funds include State Street Multi-Asset Real Return ETF, Fidelity Strategic Real Return Fund and PIMCO Inflation Response Multi-Asset Fund. The PIMCO fund's holdings include TIPS, commodities, gold and real estate investment trusts. "The idea is to have a number of different exposures so that we can have a more balanced return and not try to be so specific in getting the exact right asset class at any one moment," said Sharenow, a manager on the fund. He adds that he sees "significant value" in TIPS, which have the heaviest weighting in the portfolio. Commodities are the next largest holding. They have price "pass-throughs," which is how much companies can shift costs to customers through price increases. That is beneficial to investors, he noted. Separately, the fund holds about 10% each in gold and REITs. Draho recommends commodities, based partly on long-term asset-allocation studies that include the 1970s when inflation was far higher. "Over a long period they can help reduce risk and improve diversification," he said. "Their benefits have been most pronounced when inflation was overshooting expectations." Rather than picking individual commodities, he suggests owning a basket that's consistently rebalanced. Gold and oil, for instance, perform well in different economic and monetary policy scenarios, and it can be tricky to get the timing right.Commodity ETFs to consider include the Invesco Optimum Yield Diversified Commodity Strategy ETF (PDBC) and the iShares S&P GSCI Commodity-Indexed Trust (GSG).Another asset class Draho suggests is infrastructure — operators of roads, ports, bridges, and other hard assets. Companies in the space tend to be toll takers, collecting long-term revenue under contracts that include inflation riders or built-in price adjustments.Investors can get exposure to infrastructure through ETFs such as the iShares Global Infrastructure ETF (IGF) and ProShares DJ Brookfield Global Infrastructure ETF (TOLZ). Draho isn't sounding alarms on inflation but says it makes sense to add protection against another move higher."The risk now is there will be supply side shocks that could push up inflation again," he said. — CNBC's Daren Fonda contributed reporting.

schema.headline: Don't let inflation bite — how to hedge with TIPS, commodities and infrastructure funds
